cards.text: Job, the man from the land of Uz (Job 1:1), has just finished speaking. Now Bildad the Shuhite, one of his friends (Job 2:11), replies. He opens BIG: dominion and awe belong to God, and He establishes harmony in the heights of heaven.

cards.question: Bildad is on a roll about how great God is. He asks a question about God's troops. What does he ask?
Next Bildad asks, 'On whom does His light not rise?' Then he turns from God to people. What does Bildad ask about people?

answers.text: How can a man be just before God
Why do good people suffer so much
When will God judge the wicked

cards.text: Then Bildad points to the night sky: if even the moon does not shine and the stars are not pure in His sight... Somewhere out there, Berry is taking that VERY personally.

cards.question: True or false: Bildad says that compared to the moon and the stars, man looks more pure in God's sight.

cards.text: Bildad says how much less man, who is 'but a maggot,' and the son of man, who is 'but a worm!' Friend, I spent YEARS in the back of a junk drawer, and not ONE of the dead batteries I shared it with ever called me a maggot.
And just like that, Bildad is done. Then Job answers, and he opens with what sounds like a big compliment.

cards.question: Job tells the speaker he has saved the arm that is feeble and helped the ___.

cards.text: Then Job says, 'How you have counseled the unwise and provided fully sound insight!' I bet that's the same voice you use when a coworker 'fixes' the printer by unplugging it and walking off: 'WOW. SO helpful. Thank you SO much.'

cards.question: Job has two questions for the one who just spoke. The first is 'To whom have you uttered these words?' What is the second one about?

answers.text: Who sent you here to comfort me
Why you waited so long to speak

cards.text: Now Job starts talking about God's power, and he starts at the very bottom. The dead tremble, those beneath the waters and those who dwell in them.

cards.question: Job talks about Sheol and Abaddon and how they look before God. What does he say about Sheol?

answers.text: It is too deep for Him

cards.text: Then Job looks up. He says God stretches out the north over empty space.

cards.question: Job says God hangs the earth upon ___.

cards.text: NOTHING! I can't hang my apron on a hook without it hitting the floor, and He hangs the whole EARTH on nothing. Then Job points up at the clouds, where God wraps up the waters.

cards.question: True or false: Job says the clouds God wraps the waters in burst under their own weight.

cards.text: Remember Bildad's moon? Job has a moon too: God covers the face of the full moon, spreading His cloud over it.

cards.question: Job says God has inscribed a horizon on the face of the waters. Where does Job say that horizon sits?

answers.text: At the boundary between light and darkness
At the edge of the great deep
Where the sea meets the dry land

cards.question: True or false: Job says the foundations of heaven stand firm when God rebukes.

cards.text: Nope, they quake, astounded at His rebuke. Then Job says, 'By His power He stirred the sea; by His understanding He shattered Rahab.'

cards.question: Job says God's breath cleared the skies. He also says God's hand pierced a creature. What was it?
After everything Job just listed about God's power, how much does Job say all of it shows of God's ways?

cards.text: Then Job says, 'How faint is the whisper we hear of Him! Who then can understand the thunder of His power?' All of THAT was the whisper, friend, and trust me, Job is not done talking yet.

findings.problem: "Somewhere out there, Berry is taking that VERY personally" says what Berry is doing right now. Papa Dorin doesn't know what has happened to his kids, so this invents news about one of them.

rule.text: Never invent a reunion, any news about the kids, or any other family member.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to pick the wording of Bildad's question about God's troops ("Can they be numbered"). The baker hasn't seen that wording and can't reason it out. It tests the words of the line, not its movement or meaning.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The card gives the first half of Job's line and asks the baker to pick the wording of the second question ("Whose spirit spoke through you"). The earlier cards don't let the baker reason to it, so getting it right is a guess at the wording.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to finish the line about the horizon ("at the boundary between light and darkness"). Nothing on the earlier cards leads to it, so it is a guess at the wording.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The question itself says the horizon is inscribed "on the face of the waters." A baker could argue that the wrong answer "At the edge of the great deep" describes the same place.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: Choosing between a serpent, a lion and a wild ox is a guess at one detail of the line, like the Psalm 23 oil example. No earlier card gives context the baker could use to reason to "serpent."

rule.text: If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: "Job is not done talking yet" tells the baker what happens in the next passage: Job keeps speaking. The line should only say that the story or teaching isn't over.

rule.text: It gives nothing away about what happens next.

findings.problem: Most of Stop 2's story cards are plain retelling with none of Papa Dorin's humor (cards 1, 3 and 7, plus the opening of card 10). The apron line on card 5 is the stop's only real joke. Moments like the dead trembling, Job looking up, and Job's moon answering Bildad's moon could carry real laughs without muddying a fact.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
